title: Lines in the Sand
intro: The barcode is so common that we hardly notice it. Yet it took more than twenty-five years to travel from an inventor's idea to the supermarket checkout.

passage: Almost everything we buy today carries a small pattern of black and white lines. At the checkout, a scanner reads it in a fraction of a second, the price appears on the screen and the shop's computer records that one more item has been sold. Each code contains a number that identifies both the product and the company that made it. The barcode is so familiar that we rarely notice it, yet it took more than twenty-five years to move from a young inventor's idea to the supermarket.

The story begins in 1948 in Philadelphia, where Bernard Silver, a graduate student, overheard the head of a local chain of food shops asking a university dean for help. Checkouts were slow, prices were entered by hand and mistakes were common, so the businessman wanted a system that could record product information automatically. Silver told his friend Joseph Woodland, a recent graduate, and the two young men decided to work on the problem together.

According to the well-known story, the key moment came while Woodland was sitting on a beach in Florida. Thinking about Morse code, which he had learned as a Boy Scout, he pushed his fingers into the sand and pulled them towards him, turning the dots and dashes of the code into thin and thick lines. Because the lines could be printed in a circle, the first design looked like a target, so that it could be read from any direction. The two men applied for a patent in 1949, and it was granted in 1952.

Unfortunately, the invention was far ahead of its time. To read the code quickly, a shop would need a bright, narrow beam of light and a computer to process the information, and in the early 1950s neither was cheap or practical. Unable to develop the idea themselves, Woodland and Silver sold their patent to an electronics company for a modest sum. Silver died young, in 1963, without ever seeing his idea in use, and for many years the invention was almost forgotten.

By the late 1960s, the situation had changed. Lasers had been developed, computers were becoming smaller, and American supermarkets were under growing pressure to reduce their costs. The food industry formed a committee to choose a single standard code that every manufacturer would print on its products. Several companies submitted designs, and in 1973 the committee selected a rectangular code developed by George Laurer, an engineer at IBM, where Woodland himself was now working. The rectangular shape was easier to print accurately than the circular one. Most manufacturers were soon printing the new code on their packaging, which meant that shops could start buying scanners with confidence.

The first product to be scanned using the new system was a ten-pack of chewing gum, sold in a supermarket in Ohio in June 1974; the packet is now kept in a museum in Washington. Even then, success was not immediate. Shop owners complained that the scanners were expensive, and some customers were suspicious, worrying that shops would use the system to hide price increases. It was not until the 1980s that barcodes became common in most large shops.

Today the barcode has many descendants. In 1994, an engineer named Masahiro Hara, working for a Japanese company, developed the QR code to track car parts in factories; because it is a square made of small blocks rather than a row of lines, it can hold far more information. QR codes are now used for everything from restaurant menus to train tickets, while ordinary barcodes are used to track luggage at airports, patients in hospitals and books in libraries. Woodland, who received a national award for technology in 1992, often said that he had never imagined how far the simple lines he drew in the sand would travel.
